chapter.title: Arms and Ammunition; Parts and Accessories Thereof

page.h1: HTS Chapter 93: Arms and Ammunition; Parts and Accessories Thereof — U.S. Exports & Foreign Tariffs

seo.title: U.S. Ammunition & Firearms Exports and Foreign Tariffs (HTS Ch. 93) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: U.S. arms and ammunition exports hit $8.40B in 2025, up 32%. Who buys them (Israel, UAE, Japan, Saudi Arabia), what ships, and the tariff each buyer charges.

intro:
The U.S. exported **$8.40B** of arms and ammunition (HS Chapter 93) in 2025, up 32.3% from $6.35B in 2024 and almost double the $4.27B of 2020. Ammunition and munitions (9306) were **74%** ($6.23B), most of it other munitions and parts (9306.90, the line that includes bombs, grenades and missiles, $5.43B); military weapons (9301) added $952M and gun parts (9305) $770M, while pistols and revolvers, sporting rifles and shotguns and air guns together came to about $443M. **Israel** (23%, $1.93B) and the **United Arab Emirates** (12%, $1.00B) were the largest buyers.

Tariffs rarely decide these sales. Israel, the EU (since July 1, 2026), Australia, South Korea and Canada charge qualifying U.S. goods **nothing**; Japan charges its WTO rates of 5.4–8.4%, and the UAE and Saudi Arabia the 5% Gulf common tariff. What decides access is licensing on both sides: a **U.S. export licence** — from Commerce (BIS) for commercial firearms and ammunition, from the State Department for military items — and the **buyer’s import permit**. Canada’s 25% counter-tariff on U.S. handguns, rifles, shotguns and cartridges was lifted on September 1, 2025.

keyTakeaways: U.S. arms and ammunition exports reached $8.40B in 2025 (+32.3%); ammunition and munitions (9306) were 74% of it, and Israel, the UAE, Japan, Saudi Arabia and Germany were the five largest buyers.
Six of the 12 largest buyers charge 0% on qualifying U.S. Chapter 93 goods, the EU since July 1, 2026; Japan (5.4–8.4%), the UAE and Saudi Arabia (5%) charge their normal rates.

The only foreign tariff increase since January 2025 that hit these goods in a large market was Canada’s 25% counter-tariff on handguns, rifles, shotguns, air guns and cartridges (March 4 to September 1, 2025); an EU 30% list covering the same goods never applied.

Almost every shipment needs a U.S. export licence (BIS for commercial firearms and ammunition, the State Department for military items) and an AES filing; BIS’s 2024 tightening of firearms licences was rescinded on September 30, 2025.
